title: EU Hits AliExpress With Record €550 Million Fine for Failing to Stop Counterfeit Sales
excerpt: The largest penalty under the Digital Services Act follows fines against X and Temu, as Europe ratchets up enforcement against platforms that fail to police illegal products.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • AliExpress fined €550 million, the largest penalty under the Digital Services Act.
  • Previous fines include €120 million for X and €200 million for Temu, indicating stricter enforcement.
  • AliExpress has 193 million users in Europe and must propose remedial measures by October.
  • The company claims the fine is 'disproportionate' and is considering an appeal.
  • The European Commission fined Alibaba's AliExpress €550 million ($629 million) — the largest penalty yet under the Digital Services Act — for failing to tackle illegal, unsafe and counterfeit products.
  • The fine follows penalties of €120 million against X and €200 million against Temu, establishing a pattern of escalating DSA enforcement against major platforms.
  • AliExpress has 193 million users in Europe and faces an October deadline to propose remedial measures or risk further penalties.
  • AliExpress called the fine "disproportionate" and said it is reviewing the decision and considering all available options.

The Largest DSA Fine Yet

The European Commission dropped its heaviest Digital Services Act penalty on Monday, fining Alibaba's AliExpress €550 million ($629 million) for systematic failures in stopping the sale of counterfeit clothing, unsafe toys, dangerous cosmetics and other illegal products on its platform.

https://x.com/realTuckFrumper/status/2079264435361747153

The fine represents the third DSA enforcement action, following €120 million against Elon Musk's X in December and €200 million against Chinese e-commerce rival Temu in May. The escalating penalties signal that Brussels is moving from warnings to material financial consequences for platforms that fail to police their marketplaces.

> **"AliExpress leads with 193 million European users, followed by Shein at 156 million and Temu at 130 million."**

"AliExpress leads with 193 million European users, followed by Shein at 156 million and Temu at 130 million."

What the Commission Found

The investigation, which began in March 2024, found that AliExpress had not properly assessed whether it had sufficient staff to review potentially illegal products. The platform's detection system for identifying and removing illegal listings was deemed inadequate, with many counterfeit products and unsafe goods remaining live for weeks after being flagged, according to the Commission.

Stores that had been penalised by AliExpress for selling illegal products were able to remain active on the platform — a failure of the company's own enforcement mechanisms. The Commission also found that AliExpress had not assessed how its recommender and advertising algorithms were promoting illegal products to users.

"The spread of counterfeit clothing, unsafe toys, dangerous cosmetics and other illegal and harmful products is not an unavoidable cost of shopping online — it is a failure by AliExpress to comply with its obligations under the Digital Services Act."

— Henna Virkkunen, EU Executive Vice President for Tech

The Broader EU Crackdown

The fine is part of a pattern. One in five Europeans now shops at least monthly on AliExpress, Temu or Shein, according to EU data cited by Virkkunen. AliExpress leads with 193 million European users, followed by Shein at 156 million and Temu at 130 million. Shein faces an ongoing DSA investigation, and Temu's fine could still be increased pending further review.

The Commission has set an October 20 deadline for AliExpress to propose remedial measures. If the regulator decides in December that the measures are insufficient, additional penalties could follow.

AliExpress Responds

AliExpress called the fine "disproportionate," saying it does not adequately reflect the company's "established framework and the significant, proactive enhancements" it has made. The company said it is reviewing the decision and considering its options, including an appeal.

What This Means for Global E-Commerce

The DSA's enforcement trajectory has implications well beyond Europe. India, which has its own challenges with counterfeit products on domestic and cross-border e-commerce platforms, may look to the EU's regulatory framework as a template for its evolving digital marketplace rules. For consumers globally, the question is whether financial penalties of this scale can actually change platform behaviour — or whether they become a cost of doing business in markets too large to ignore.
